entries.title: Senate Republicans Are Now Pushing for More of a Say in Iran War
entries.summary: Lawmakers worry about escalating war amid troop deaths and rising energy prices.
entries.content:
Republican senators are pressing the Trump administration to offer a clearer plan and more information about the Iran war after three U.S. service members were killed and dozens were wounded in renewed attacks in recent days.

Several lawmakers said Monday that Congress should no longer remain on the sidelines and that the White House needs to explain where the conflict is headed.

“It looked like things were tapering off, and now things look like they’re heating up,” Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-Louisiana) told NOTUS.

The fighting intensified over the weekend after Iranian attacks killed two U.S. soldiers at a base in Jordan. A third service member was killed in Iraq during the controlled detonation of an Iranian drone. The U.S. military said Monday it was carrying out a 10th consecutive night of strikes against Iran. Trump vowed further retaliation Monday.

Cassidy said the latest escalation warrants congressional briefings, individual briefings and “the president speaking to the American people about it, explaining the circumstances,”

“I think some sort of authorization of force should be part of that,” Cassidy said, before stopping short of endorsing formally adopting an AUMF. “I just know Congress needs to be involved.”

Adding to the troubles is that gas prices are on the rise once again. Prices per gallon eclipsed $4.50 on average in May, but that figure was on the decline until July 4th. Since then, gas prices have sharply increased to nearly $4 per gallon as Iran has again choked off the Strait of Hormuz.

“That, to me, is the key consideration in all of this,” Senate Majority Leader John Thune told reporters. “That’s going to be key to all these economic questions that have been raised.”

No briefing from administration officials appears imminent. Thune told NOTUS that he does not expect a briefing this week.

“I don’t know that I expect to,” Thune told NOTUS. “Anytime where we’ve got kinetic activity over there, regular updates are helpful.”

Some new information could come tomorrow. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Chair of the Joint Chiefs Dan Caine will appear before the Senate Appropriations Committee on Tuesday, where they are expected to answer questions about the Trump administration’s $87.6 billion supplemental request for Iran war funding.

Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) said Congress should be more involved in approving the war.

“I think it’s clear that it is time for Congress to act,” Curtis said. “And that doesn’t mean that it’s necessarily acting, constraining the president, but in fact defining what this looks like.”

Curtis said Congress should consider a formal declaration of war on a narrower authorization for specific military action.

Sen. Thom Tillis (R-North Carolina) said the renewed fighting on July 10 started a new 60-day clock under the War Powers Resolution.

“My 60-day clock is ticking.” Tillis said.

But not every Republican calling for a clearer plan wants restraint.

Sen. Mike Rounds (R-South Dakota) said the administration needs a strategy to break the cycle of Iranian attacks and U.S. retaliation beyond “just hoping for a diplomatic outcome.”

“It may very well mean having a plan to militarily resolve this situation,” Rounds said. He added that senators should receive classified briefings.

Sen. Roger Wicker (R-Mississippi), the chair of the Senate Armed Services Committee, echoed Round’s call for a more decisive approach.

“I just hope we go ahead and finish the job in Iran,” Wicker said.

At issue for members is the timeline. The fighting in Iran kicked off in late February, with lawmakers on both sides of the aisle wanting a swift resolution to the war that Trump and administration officials insisted would only go on for a matter of weeks, not months.

The “memorandum of understanding” last month brought a temporary halt to activity between the two sides, but has since been brushed aside, leading to the renewed hostilities and worrying lawmakers.

“We've lost soldiers. That's a new, very concerning, sad development,” said Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-West Virginia). “The escalation's concerning.”

“You don’t know which way it's going to go,” she added.

Meanwhile, Democrats plan to force another vote in the Senate this week to cut off hostilities with Iran, aiming to put added pressure on vulnerable Republicans ahead of November’s midterm elections. Last month, four Republican senators broke party lines to support a similar war powers resolution, which was symbolic and not legally binding.

“Trump needs to stop this catastrophe and bring our troops home, and Senate Republicans can’t let him off the hook until he does,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said in a floor speech Monday announcing the vote.

Sen. Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii) urged Republicans who have concerns about the war to join Democrats in voting for the measure and fulfill their responsibilities as a coequal branch of government.

“You can't be against this war and then keep voting to fund the war, and you can't be against this war and keep rejecting these war powers resolutions,” Schatz told NOTUS.

Senate Democrats also blocked an effort to begin debate on the annual defense policy bill last week in protest of the Iran war.

“Every time Iran kills an American Soldier they will pay for that killing many times over!” Trump wrote Monday on Truth Social.
entries.author: Hamed Ahmadi, Al Weaver, Igor Bobic

entries.title: Democrats Ditch Their Old Pick in a Competitive Arizona Seat
entries.summary: The DCCC is supporting Marlene Galán-Woods in her primary, even though she’s running against Amish Shah, the candidate it backed in the 2024 general election.
entries.content:
Voters in Arizona’s 1st Congressional District are looking at something of a rematch in their Democratic primary. Unlike in 2024, when House Democrats’ campaign arm let the race play out, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee now has a clear preference.

The group’s pick in the primary is Marlene Galán-Woods, a former broadcast journalist who has never held public office, was registered as a Republican until 2018 and came in third when she ran in 2024. On Tuesday, she’ll face off against several Democrats, including Amish Shah, an emergency-room physician and former state legislator who beat her in the primary in 2024 and competed in the general election with the DCCC’s backing.

Shah narrowly lost to Republican Rep. David Schweikert in 2024. This year, the DCCC hopes Democrats in the district will choose not to give Shah a do-over, but to go in a new direction with Galán-Woods. While the DCCC put Shah on its Red to Blue list in the 2024 general election but did not intervene in that year’s primary, now it’s Galán-Woods who’s in the DCCC’s Red to Blue program.

“She’s on paper a better fit, but you're dealing with the rather uncomfortable question that she already lost a primary to him,” said a Democratic strategist and DCCC alum who has worked on previous races in the district. “So, was it a resource problem? Was there something else that has changed? No doubt that DCCC has analyzed this, weighed all of this, and still come to the conclusion that intervention enhances their odds of picking up a seat.”

The candidates have few ideological differences and are running in the country’s only open toss-up seat, since Schweikert is running for governor. The Democratic race is one of several primaries the DCCC has weighed in on, along with contests in Pennsylvania and Texas battleground districts.

This type of intervention in competitive primaries has prompted backlash from some corners of the party, who say the committee should let voters decide rather than putting its thumb on the scale.

“It's unfair because out of respect to him for winning such a competitive 2024 primary, I think they should have either stayed out or at least waited until after the primary,” said Arizona state Sen. Flavio Bravo, who endorsed Shah.

So far this year, most of the DCCC’s picks have succeeded in their primary races, but two candidates have lost: state Sen. Joe Baldacci in Maine’s 2nd Congressional District and Assemblymember Jasmeet Bains in California’s 22nd Congressional District. Those losses left some Democrats questioning the committee's use of resources and cheering the defeat of the establishment.

This Arizona race has become another test for the DCCC in a primary that lacks the progressive-versus-pragmatic dynamic that has defined other races.

“Unless there is a clear and obvious reason, the DCCC should not intervene in Democratic primaries, including the race in AZ-01,” said Rep. Adelita Grijalva (D-Arizona) in a statement to NOTUS. “These resources should be focused on flipping this seat in November and winning back the House majority.”

Shah was frustrated about the DCCC’s decision to weigh in.

“I think they got it wrong,” he told NOTUS. “I think the Democratic Party voters do not want to see meddling from D.C. here in our district.”

If he pulls off a win, he said he will “work with anybody and everybody, including the DCCC, to make sure that we do everything we can to stop this guy in the White House.”

The DCCC determined that Galán-Woods has “undeniable momentum, a broad coalition, and strong fundraising,” a spokesperson said.

“This designation signifies that we believe this candidate — and this campaign — are the one best positioned to flip the Republican-held district,” the spokesperson said.

Galán-Woods has accumulated support from other major players in the party. She received a powerful endorsement from Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly in the final days before the primary. She also has the backing of several national Democratic groups including Planned Parenthood Action Fund, EMILYs List, the Bench and BOLD PAC. 

She’s proved herself to be an effective fundraiser, raising about $2.1 million as of July 1, according to Federal Election Commission filings, compared to Shah’s $1.3 million. She also has allies spending mountains of money on her behalf, far outpacing the spending on Shah’s behalf.

Galán-Woods said she decided to run again because Shah, who lost the general election by 4 percentage points, underperformed Kamala Harris and Ruben Gallego in 2024’s presidential and Senate contests.

When asked about the DCCC’s backing, Galán-Woods said she’s most proud of her local backing.

“I'm happy to have the support, but I'll be honest with you, here in the district, people aren't talking about it,” she said. “People are talking about the issues that keep them up at night, and most importantly, how do we win? How do we win in November?”

There’s been limited polling in the primary. HighGround, a public affairs firm that has worked on Republican campaigns, showed Shah up by 22 percentage points in a February poll. Most voters in the district are registered Republicans, but voters who did not select a party at all outnumber Democrats.

“This district is a really good bellwether for how the country's going,” said Eric Chalmers, a Democratic strategist in Arizona not involved in the race. “The independents who live in this district, they went one way for three cycles voting for Dems, and then last cycle, it was almost a complete 180.”

Some Democrats see Galán-Woods — who grew up in a Republican household with parents who emigrated from Cuba and who is the widow of Grant Woods, the former Republican state attorney general and chief of staff to John McCain — as just the right kind of Democrat to win over independents.

“The appeal of a different candidate who's got a lot of support from the business community and a lot of the ‘Republican-lites’ or kind of McCain-Republican types out in CD 1, which makes up a lot of that district, led to the appeal of wanting to try Marlene,” Chalmers said.

Shah, meanwhile, is pitching himself as an experienced politician. He served in the statehouse for three terms and ran in the general election before, while Galán-Woods lacks public office experience.

He is known for his shoeleather campaign style and touts that he’s knocked on 28,000 doors in the district. But Arizona strategists said he will have to scale it up.

“On paper he's just a normie Democrat with a really interesting, compelling background and compelling voice,” said DJ Quinlan, a Democratic strategist in Arizona not working on the race. “In practice on the campaign trail, he has a number of unique views.”

Quinlan said one of Shah’s challenges is his apparent dislike of negative campaigning and TV ads.

“He seems to have an aversion to the sort of campaign tactics that you need to be successful as you scale from a legislative race to a congressional race,” he said.

Shah, however, calls that a mischaracterization. He pointed to his 2024 fundraising numbers and television ads to show that his last campaign did put up a congressional-level fight. Door-knocking helps the campaign keep an ear to the ground, he said.

“We understood in 2024 that there's no way that you could run a door-knocking campaign over the course of six or eight weeks directed at 500,000 people,” Shah said. “That was nowhere in my arguments. We ran a mass communication campaign that involved mailers, that involved TV ads, that involved digital, all at the direction of the DCCC during that 2024 cycle.”

The primary’s winner will advance to face either former state Rep. Joseph Chaplik, business executive John Trobough, or the Trump-endorsed former NFL kicker Jay Feely.
entries.author: Christa Dutton

entries.title: What $1 Million Gets You in D.C., Maryland and Virginia (With a Pool!)
entries.summary: Our weekly column compares home listings across the metro area.
entries.content:
It’s summer, D.C. is steamier than a crab pot, and even casual Zillow browsers might be thinking: If only I could step straight out my door and into a pool.

For NOTUS’ inaugural D/M/V real estate column, we found listings in the District, Maryland and Virginia that, for a million dollars, will make that dream a backyard reality.

One caveat: Getting a pool of your own in the District isn’t easy for a cool million. (Although, for $15 million, this seven-bedroom compound in Georgetown comes with a courtyard pool.) So, we found what we think is the closest thing.

Here are three homes we found priced at a million dollars and ideal for anyone prioritizing pool access as they house-hunt.

(Which one would you choose? Or, have a comparison you’d like to see in an upcoming column? Let us know at metro@notus.com.)

D.C.

The listing: 3287 Sutton Place NW, Unit D

The price: $950,000
UntitledThe specifics: A two-bedroom, two-story, three-bathroom townhome with a private courtyard. Built in 1980 but recently renovated with fresh paint and white trim throughout.

The pool: Shared between just 42 homes, the Sutton Place pool is perfect for splashing, lap-swimming or relaxing. Be sure to budget for $790 a month in condo fees.

Sell us on it: “Private community pools are a rarity in Northwest, D.C., especially for homes around the $1 million price point,” said Northgate real estate agent Ilse Padron, who also noted the location is “just minutes from Cathedral Commons, Georgetown, downtown D.C. and some of the city's top public and private schools.”

Maryland

The listing: 12320 Putters Ct, Upper Marlboro, Md.

The price: $1,099,900

Untitled
The specifics: The former third home for a family of jet-setters, this property functions like a year-round resort, with an outdoor pool to enjoy in the summer. Prefer the après-ski lifestyle? You’ll enjoy the patio jacuzzi, indoor sauna and multiple fireplaces. The walk-out finished basement currently houses a gym, perfect for a pre-swim workout. There’s no HOA fees, but the Marlton Golf Club is just on the other side of the woods for anyone who wants to hit the greens. (Hence the road name, Putter’s Court.)

The pool: Surrounded by a wrought-iron fence, and with woods rimming the nearly four-acre lot, the pool feels extra private. There’s a lengthy shelf perfect for splashing toddlers, and on the opposite side, built-in bar stools for adult swim.

Sell us on it: “I can’t believe this home is still on the market,” said broker Tina Marie Marshall, adding: “The owners kept it immaculate. We barely had to stage it, this is how they lived.”

Virginia

The listing: 3227 Annandale Road, Falls Church, Va.

The price: $1,095,000
UntitledThe specifics: Who needs a large house when you have a pool house? This modest, three-bedroom, brick Cape Cod is all business in the front yard and party in the back. A stone patio connects the main house with a pool house, creating additional year-round space for noisy kids or a quiet work-from-home office, depending on your family’s needs.

The pool: Surrounded by willow trees and other lush landscaping, this in-ground pool has a new companion salt-water spa added in 2022.

Sell us on it: “You're not just buying a house; you're buying an excuse to cancel your vacation plans,” said Compass listing agent Ana Maria Menendez. “You're going to be … wondering why you ever paid resort prices when your own backyard feels better.”
entries.author: Rebecca Ritzel

entries.title: Will Incoming Progressives Give Hakeem Jeffries Their Support?
entries.summary: Brad Lander backed his New York colleague but warned that “voters are fed up with the status quo.”
entries.content:
New York’s Brad Lander said he would support House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries for speaker if Democrats win back the House — an olive branch from a candidate expected to become one of Congress’ highest-profile progressives.

Lander and several likely members of Congress — including Melat Kiros, Darializa Avila Chevalier, Claire Valdez and Chris Rabb — are part of a group of uber-progressive Democrats, many aligned with the leftist Democratic Socialists of America, who recently won competitive primaries in safe blue districts. The majority of them have not committed to supporting Jeffries if Democrats win in November.

Lander’s support for Jeffries, who is a fellow New Yorker, is a tacit admission that the members are willing to give leadership a chance as they’re on the cusp of winning back the majority — but still he warned that “voters are fed up with the status quo.”

“I look forward to voting for Hakeem to be the speaker of the House,” Lander said in a recent interview with NOTUS. “At the same time, I want a party and party leadership that can listen to the passion and anger that voters feel and be responsive to it, and that means showing people much more clearly than leadership have so far what we're fighting for.”

DSA-aligned candidates built their campaigns around a direct challenge to the Democratic Party’s “status quo,” casting themselves as insurgents willing to break with establishment leadership. Their message centered on economic populism — even when that meant taking on moderate Democrats rather than Republicans.

Now that several of them are on track to easily win in November, the tug-of-war over the Democratic caucus’s center of gravity is about to grow even more pronounced. And many of the people who will be trying to pull it left will be from congressional districts in Jeffries’ backyard.

Landers has previously said he plans to support Jeffries for speaker.

"There will be a good opportunity for leadership to create a framework in which we can cut the line as fighters versus folders and show that it will be possible to win the majority in a strong way and to hear what voters are saying about their frustrations and the bolder posture they want to see from Democrats,” Lander, who beat incumbent Rep. Dan Goldman in a primary that attracted national attention, told NOTUS.

Lander said Jeffries called to congratulate him and that the two have continued to talk, along with Jeffries' team, about how Jeffries envisions progressives working in the next Congress.

When asked for comment, Jeffries team pointed to his remarks at a recent press conference.

“I've talked to several of them, and we'll have more to say about it in the future,” Jeffries told reporters when asked about the winners of the competitive primaries in his home state.

Building new working relationships between drastically different wings of the party isn’t an entirely new dynamic for Democratic lawmakers to navigate. In 2019, after Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Ilhan Omar, Rashida Tlaib and Ayanna Pressley arrived as the “Squad,” the then-new lawmakers had to establish a working relationship with then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi.

They often broke with leadership on marquee votes, including when Omar and Tlaib opposed the 2021 bipartisan infrastructure bill, and several backed primary challenges against sitting Democratic incumbents in the years that followed.

Pelosi, who’s retiring, said she has no concerns for Jeffries after November.

“Hakeem is a very unifying force. He's eloquent. He listens,” Pelosi said in an interview. “He's very respected by the members. I was a different kind of voice, and I always had a race, except for my first time. Every single time I had a race. I don't see that for him. I think he will have a very unified caucus.”

Ocasio-Cortez, who told NOTUS she’s made herself a resource for the incoming members, said she understands the candidates have to listen to their constituents who elected them for change.

“Movement-based candidates don't just make individual calculations. Movement-based candidates generally try to be — especially when they're elected from their communities — I think they just conference a lot with their communities,” she said.

Some centrist lawmakers, however, are already concerned that the DSA-aligned candidates will use tactics similar to those used by conservatives in the House Republican Conference, whether it be voting down a rule or refusing to back measures supported by moderate Democrats.

Rep. Brad Schneider, chair of the centrist New Democrat Coalition, which has more than 100 Democratic members, argued there should be more attention to the moderate candidates running in battleground races. He argued that candidates like the ones who have beat out incumbents are “not adding to the Democratic majority” because they’re in already-blue districts.

“I am concerned about the rhetoric when [the progressives] come in and they say, ‘We are going to take down the rules, take down the speaker,’ and do these things,” Schneider said. “That just locks it up. We see that with the Republicans.”

While none of the soon-to-be members of Congress have said they plan to vote against Jeffries, they’re noncommittal about supporting him.

Several progressives said the fear expressed by Schneider is disconnected from reality.

“I think if their fear is simply that these will be people who are more interested in division for its own sake or attention for its own sake, they've got something else coming,” said Andrew Bard Epstein, who worked on New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s campaign and Valdez’s campaign. (Mamdani backed several of the New York progressives on track to win seats in Congress.) “These are people who are smart and determined and strategic.”

Lander was optimistic that in the general election, once primaries are wrapped up, Democrats will come together to win the majority. He dismissed any concerns about members of the caucus being able to work together in that scenario.

"I'm much more worried about Donald Trump and the danger that he presents to the country than I am about the divisions within the party," he said.
entries.author: Daniella Diaz

entries.title: Andy Kim’s Big Health Care Pitch: Enroll Every Kid in Medicaid
entries.summary: The New Jersey senator takes a unique, long-game approach to a top Democratic goal.
entries.content:
Sen. Andy Kim is taking a unique approach to the Senate.

The New Jersey Democrat is trying to spark a debate about how to achieve a very-long-sought goal of his party — universal health care — while blending it with a long-term outlook that might take years or even decades to fully achieve.

“I'm trying to think through everything I can do for the next two-and-a-half years. But I'm also thinking through the next two-and-a-half decades,” Kim, 44, who is 18 months into his first Senate term, told NOTUS in an interview. “What do I want to accomplish here, what is the type of senator I want to be? And I think this is, particularly, very meaningful.”

On Tuesday, Kim is introducing the MediKids Act, which would effectively enroll every child into a section of Medicaid that is already used to provide health services for children from lower-income families.

The legislation, which does not yet have a full cost estimate, would fully fund health coverage for children from birth until age 26. Families would be free to opt out of the federally funded health insurance if they wanted different plans in the private sector, but the impact could be similar to how Medicare takes care of seniors once they turn 65.

Kim described his proposal as creating “bookends” for the most critical years: federally guaranteed health coverage from birth to 25 and 65 till death, about half of the average American life of 79 years.

Health experts estimate that 6% of children under 18, about 4.5 million, do not have any health insurance. Kim said that another 23 million are “under insured.”

Kim’s ultimate goal, however, is to have members of his party think bigger and more realistically about the drive to achieve the elusive Democratic dream of universal health care — an “Odyssey”-like endeavor that began at least in the early 1940s when John Dingell Sr. introduced the first national health-care bill. For the last decade the party has been battling over progressive demands of creating “Medicare for All” versus the more mainstream approach of expanding on the landmark 2010 Affordable Care Act.

The ACA helped drive down the number of uninsured from about 46 million in 2010 to roughly 26 million, according to KFF, an independent health-research firm.

Republicans have enjoyed the Democratic infighting over those competing ideas and, as far back as 2018, have used political hit ads calling “Medicare for All” a “massive government-run system” that would force Americans off health-care plans they like.

Kim is trying to create a different approach that takes the politically safer ground of guaranteeing health care for children.

“It’s the clearest point to be made about the need for universal health care and the idea that health care is a human right,” Kim said. “I really hope that none of my colleagues will really look me in the eye and say they don't think every child should get health care in this country.”

Kim is not the first name insiders would expect to try to lead a new health-care effort. He’s one of the most junior members of the Senate health committee and does not have a seat on the Finance Committee, which has jurisdiction over Medicare and Medicaid.

But the Rhodes scholar and foreign-policy expert who worked in the State Department, Pentagon and on then-President Barack Obama’s National Security Council holds an unusual set of crossover credentials among Democrats. He has both won a battleground district and earned plaudits from the online progressive orbit.

He launched his political career in 2017 when one of his children was born with a preexisting medical condition, at a time when congressional Republicans advanced legislation to repeal the ACA and end protections for those with such a condition. Their push ultimately fell short.

“That anxiety that I felt as a parent was gut-wrenching. I don't believe that there's anything more fearful, parents are more scared of, than their kid being sick,” he said.

After winning a Republican-held district to the east of Philadelphia, he became a pragmatic Democrat along with other House freshmen who had national-security backgrounds. One ideological ranking of his first-term placed Kim among the 30 most conservative in his caucus.

He went viral on the night of Jan. 6, 2021, when pictures spread of him on his hands and knees cleaning up the Capitol after the attack.

By 2023, after then-Sen. Bob Menendez (D-New Jersey) was indicted on corruption charges, Kim jumped into the Senate race against the wishes of the state’s seemingly entrenched establishment. He went to the Senate and upended the state’s power structure, while Menendez is now serving a federal prison sentence.

He’s not currently planning any bids for caucus leadership positions. He is, under current caucus rules, at least a decade or two away from chairing an influential committee.

He does not try to react to every big scandal or controversy of the moment, which is the usual path these days to cable TV hits and large social media followings. Instead, he is the rare senator who has plotted out long-term plans, sometimes even charting out 10-year objectives.

“I'm gonna be in this fight for as long as it takes. I just doubled the number of millennials here in the Senate on the Democratic side single-handedly,” he said.

The other Democratic millennial, Sen. Jon Ossoff of Georgia, has liberals swooning online with every clip of his reelection-campaign speeches, drawing talk of a 2028 presidential bid.

A diminutive son of Korean immigrants, Kim is not planning a presidential bid. Representing a blue state like New Jersey, he could serve in the Senate for decades to come.

“This is my life's work,” he said of his new legislation.

Kim counts himself among the Democrats who believe that Trump has given them an opportunity to reenvision federal government programs. If Democrats gain full power, he doesn’t want to just recreate the U.S. Agency for International Development or restore cuts to Medicaid that came as part of the Republican 2025 domestic policy bill.

“Part of why Trump got elected is people were frustrated with the status quo,” he said. “They thought it was broken, and we need to show that, look, I also believe that the status quo is fundamentally broken, but here is a real idea that could have immeasurable impact.”

His MediKids proposal starts off with three Democratic co-sponsors: Sens. Cory Booker of New Jersey, Tammy Duckworth of Illinois and Alex Padilla of California.

Voters have a complicated view of government involvement in health care, as two liberal-leaning groups, the Searchlight Institute and Zeteo, found in a study released this month. Fewer than four-in-10 Democrats have confidence in the federal government to run a national health-insurance plan.

This issue has been the Democratic dream for decades. In 1971, after Sen. Robert Byrd of West Virginia defeated Sen. Ted Kennedy of Massachusetts for Democratic whip, Kennedy told reporters he would dedicate himself to the “cause of my life,” universal health care.

It took 38 years for the ACA to get passed and signed into law, six months after Kennedy died.

Kim already said in his inaugural speech on the Senate floor that his farewell address will include an assessment of whether he succeeded in expanding health care.

“I hope it doesn't take that long because that would be a real detriment to the American people,” he said. “But for as long as I'm here, I'm going to be pushing on these ideas.”
entries.author: Paul Kane

entries.title: Fetterman's Ultimatum Giving Some Democrats Anxiety He’ll Switch Parties
entries.summary: The Pennsylvania Democrat warns he will leave the party if it officially changes its platform regarding its stance toward Israel.
entries.content:
Sen. John Fetterman’s increasingly independent political moves are raising eyebrows among his Senate colleagues and giving fodder to his progressive critics, fueling speculation about whether he might leave the Democratic Party.

Fetterman said last week he would formally switch his affiliation if Democrats make opposition to Israel part of their official platform. It’s the first time the Pennsylvania senator has laid out a scenario in which he would jump ship.

Fetterman’s colleagues have doubts about his ability to win a Democratic primary. One Democratic senator, who requested anonymity to speak freely, expressed anxiety over the prospect of an unexpected party switch by Fetterman.

“I am concerned,” the senator told NOTUS.

Fetterman has pointed to recent contested primaries as evidence that the party is changing.

“Look at the kinds of people that are winning our primaries. Not just, ‘I'm pro-Palestinian,’ but, ‘I'm intensely anti-Israel.’ That's a significant difference,” Fetterman told NOTUS.

His decision to set up a joint fundraising committee with Republican Sen. Dave McCormick, his Pennsylvania colleague with whom he shares a uniquely close bipartisan friendship, is also raising questions. Joint fundraising committees are a common way to bulk up one’s coffers, but it’s highly unusual for participants to be affiliated with different political parties, a move that didn’t go unnoticed by his colleagues in the Senate.

“I've never seen it before. Yes, I'm struck by it,” Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Maryland), who served as chair of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, told NOTUS.

Rep. Chris Deluzio (D-Pennsylvania), a progressive who has left the door open to a potential challenge to Fetterman once his term expires in 2028, called Fetterman’s decision to team up with McCormick on fundraising “crazy stuff.”

“We have battleground races in Pennsylvania that we are trying to flip, and now we’ve got John Fetterman helping the Republicans to raise money to beat Democrats,” Deluzio told MeidasTouch last week.

Asked to respond to Deluzio, Fetterman told NOTUS the congressman “shouldn’t criticize” because he donated money to “an accused rapist,” referring to Graham Platner, who dropped out of the Maine Senate race earlier this month following an allegation of sexual assault, something Platner denied. Deluzio’s political action committee, Yinzer PAC, gave $500 to Platner’s campaign in March, before the allegations against Platner were made public.

Fetterman downplayed the joint fundraising committee with McCormick, telling the the Washington Examiner, “It’s nothing sinister.”

“It’s just — people have joint interest in the things that we happen to agree on, if we both represent Pennsylvania,” he told the outlet.

Fetterman has increasingly found himself isolated in the Democratic Party. Although he votes with Democrats on most bills and nominations, his staunch support for Israel, the Iran war and border security has irked some in his party. He seems to relish attacking Democrats, most recently lambasting progressives for their decision to back Platner in Maine’s Senate race.

Last month, Fetterman expressed regret for calling to eliminate the filibuster during his 2022 Senate run and praised former Democratic Sens. Joe Manchin and Kyrsten Sinema for defending the Senate’s long-standing supermajority requirement under President Joe Biden’s tenure.

“If we lose the filibuster, then the rights of the minority, whether that will be Democrat or Republican minority, would have effectively little to no voice,” Fetterman said in an interview with conservative podcast host Katie Miller, the wife of White House adviser Stephen Miller. “And if we become a smaller version of the House, that would have profound ramifications for the United States, and that would be dangerous. I'll be the first to say that our entire Democratic Party was wrong about that in that cycle."

Fetterman’s approval ratings in Pennsylvania have fallen to 19% among Democrats, according to a Quinnipiac University poll released last week. The same survey found that 52% of voters want Fetterman to leave the party.

The senator told CNN he couldn’t explain how “a guy that votes 90% on the Democratic line [has] 80% GOP approval. He added: “If I'm becoming more unpopular with Democrats, that's a strong correlation of being a proud Israel supporter.”

Asked if he thought he could win a Democratic primary, Fetterman said, “I guess we’ll see.” He hasn’t announced whether he will seek another term.

Adam Jentleson, Fetterman’s former chief of staff and founder of the Searchlight Institute, a Democratic think tank, said he believed the senator might leave the party “in order to stay relevant,” particularly in a scenario where Democrats win a Senate majority by a single seat in November.

“I think, if he is the majority-maker, he will flip, because it would give him a massive amount of attention,” Jentleson, who last year expressed concerns about his former boss’ mental health, said in an interview with NOTUS.

Jentleson said the real risk for Democrats is if a vacancy opens up on the Supreme Court. Fetterman recently voted to confirm former Sen. Markwayne Mullin as Trump’s Homeland Security secretary, so he could cross the aisle again to back a future Trump Supreme Court nomination.

“I would be the first to say that Senate seats are invaluable, but Democrats should not debase themselves by trying to negotiate with him,” Jentleson added. “If he switches, it’s containable — it will be a problem for two years but we can recoup it in 2028.”

Other Democrats were skeptical about the idea of Fetterman becoming a Republican, noting he maintains progressive policy positions on key social issues including abortion, marijuana and LGBTQ+ rights.

“He votes Democratic all the time. I mean, he'd be a bad Republican,” Vermont Sen. Peter Welch, who is friendly with Fetterman, told NOTUS.

New Mexico Sen. Martin Heinrich urged Fetterman not to leave the party.

“I would just encourage him to stay,” Heinrich said. “I think you can have policy differences, but on balance, with the exception of one or two issues, when you look at what he cares about, I think that looks a lot more like the Democratic Party than the Republican Party. He's always, always welcome in our caucus.”

Maine Sen. Angus King, an independent who caucuses with Democrats, said the “water’s OK” on charting a different path in the Senate.

“The Democratic Party has been very good to me, allowing me to develop seniority on committees, work on the committees I’m interested in,” King said.

Sen. Steve Daines (R-Montana), the former head of his party’s Senate campaign arm, said he found Fetterman joining the Republican conference “unlikely,” but he agreed it would be tough for him to win reelection in Pennsylvania as a Democrat.

“I applaud his moral clarity and his courage, and that's greatly respected by voters on both sides. But it would be hard to run in a Democrat primary now,” Daines said.

History wouldn’t be on Fetterman’s side if he does decide to leave the party. When then-Pennsylvania Sen. Arlen Specter, a moderate, left the Republican Party ahead of anticipated GOP primary loss in 2010, he provided Democrats a crucial 60th vote in the Senate, allowing them to ultimately pass the Affordable Care Act, the landmark health care law. But Specter’s party switch and his vote for Obamacare didn’t save him in the end. He went on to lose in the Democratic primary against then-Rep. Joe Sestak.

Berwood Yost, director of the Floyd Institute for Public Policy at Franklin & Marshall College, said Fetterman is listening to voters in a battleground state like Pennsylvania who want their elected officials to reach across the aisle. But Yost said the strategy might backfire in the current partisan political environment.

“He’s had appeal with voters many Democrats are interested in winning back,” Yost said in an interview with NOTUS. “His political brand has always been snarky — cynical in some ways. Some people read him as progressive, but he’s always been his own brand.”

“I think it’s more likely he would become —declare himself an independent — but that hasn’t worked in Pennsylvania,” Yost added. “He finds himself in a place of his own making.”
